Siege
seej
n. (the surrounding of a city by an army to reduce it; rendering Hebrew matsor, from tsur, to bind or besiege)
From Old French sege, a seat, from the Latin sedeo, to sit — an army sits down before a city. The buried image is patience rather than assault: a siege wins by staying.

Biblical Definition

A siege in Scripture is judgment made slow. Ezekiel is commanded to act one out in miniature against a tile: “lay siege against it, and build a fort against it, and cast a mount against it; set the camp also against it, and set battering rams against it round about” (Ezekiel 4:2). The prophet becomes the besieger of his own city, and the accumulation of clauses is the point — a siege is methodical, and Jerusalem's fall would be too. Isaiah puts the LORD himself in the besieger's place: “I will camp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with a mount” (Isaiah 29:3). This is the hardest fact about the sieges of the Old Testament: the army outside the wall is often God's instrument against his own people, and the walls that were meant to keep enemies out become the enclosure of a judgment. The historian records the end without adornment: “And the city was besieged unto the eleventh year of king Zedekiah” (2 Kings 25:2) — one sentence covering months of famine. Micah writes from inside one: “he hath laid siege against us: they shall smite the judge of Israel with a rod upon the cheek” (Micah 5:1). The very next verse names Bethlehem and the ruler whose goings forth have been from everlasting. The promise of Christ is given to a people under siege.

Webster 1828 Definition

The sitting-down of an army before a city. In Scripture it is judgment made slow and methodical, often with the LORD himself named as the besieger of his own city — and Micah announces Bethlehem from inside one.

expand to see more

SIEGE, n. [Fr. siege, a seat; L. sedeo, to sit.] The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling the garrison to surrender.

2. Any continued endeavor to gain possession.

3. Formerly, a seat; a throne; hence, rank; place; class.

4. To lay siege, to besiege; to beset with an armed force.

5. To raise a siege, to relinquish an attempt to take a place by besieging it.

Key Scripture

Ezekiel 4:2 — "And lay siege against it, and build a fort against it, and cast a mount against it; set the camp also against it, and set battering rams against it round about."

Isaiah 29:3 — "And I will camp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with a mount, and I will raise forts against thee."

2 Kings 25:2 — "And the city was besieged unto the eleventh year of king Zedekiah."

Micah 5:1 — "Now gather thyself in troops, O daughter of troops: he hath laid siege against us: they shall smite the judge of Israel with a rod upon the cheek."

Modern Corruption

The sieges of Scripture are read as ancient military history rather than as the covenant sanctions God warned of by name — and the God who besieges his own city is quietly replaced by one who only ever rescues.

expand to see more

Deuteronomy 28 lists siege among the covenant curses in appalling detail, centuries before Nebuchadnezzar's engineers arrived, and Leviticus 26 does the same. When the Babylonian mount went up against Jerusalem it was not an accident of geopolitics but the arrival of a stated sanction. Modern readings that treat these narratives as the ordinary fate of small kingdoms between empires lose exactly what the prophets insisted on — that Israel's political history was covenantal, and that the besieging army was a rod in the hand of her God. Isaiah 29:3 will not let the reader escape it: the speaker who camps against Ariel round about is the LORD.

The principle to recover is where the promise falls. Micah 5:1 describes a judge of Israel struck on the cheek with a rod while the enemy sits outside the wall; Micah 5:2 announces the everlasting ruler to come out of Bethlehem Ephratah. God gives his brightest promise to a people at their lowest, and does not wait for the siege to lift before speaking of the Messiah. A church that has learned to read sieges rightly will neither pretend the judgment is not real nor conclude that God has finished with the city he is chastening.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew matsor is a siege or the works of one, from tsur, to bind, confine, besiege. Dayeq is the siege-wall thrown up; solelah, the mount cast against a wall.

expand to see more

Hebrew matsor (H4692) — a siege, an entrenchment; from tsur, to bind or hem in.

Hebrew tsur (H6696) — to bind, besiege, confine; the verb of laying siege.

Hebrew solelah (H5550) — a mount or ramp cast up against a city wall.

Hebrew dayeq (H1785) — a siege-wall or watchtower built by the besiegers.

Hebrew kar (H3733) — a battering ram, among the engines set against a wall in Ezekiel 4:2.

Usage

"Of a siege enacted in miniature: lay siege against it, and build a fort against it (Ezekiel 4:2)."

"Of the LORD as the besieger: I will camp against thee round about (Isaiah 29:3)."

"Of the plain historical end: the city was besieged unto the eleventh year of king Zedekiah (2 Kings 25:2)."
